newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-YEGOROVA STRIPPED OF GOLD MEDAL FOR DOPING.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-YEGOROVA STRIPPED OF GOLD MEDAL FOR DOPING.

text.p: Russian Lyubov Yegorova tested positive after her victory in Sunday's 5-km classic cross-country race and was stripped of her world title and excluded from the Nordic skiing world championships.

International Ski Federation (FIS) general secretary Gian Franco Kasper said on Wednesday a urine sample analysed by an Oslo laboratory accredited by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) showed Yegorova had taken Bromantan, a banned stimulant-cum masking agent.
When informed by the Russian Federation about the positive test, Yegorova admitted taking the substance and said it was her own decision and she was the only one responsible for taking it.
"As she admitted taking the banned substance, a second test on the B-sample was not necessary," Kasper said.
Positive dope tests must be confirmed by tests on a second sample unless the athlete admits wrongdoing.

Yegorova, 30, six times an Olympic champion and three times a world champion before coming to Trondheim, was automatically disqualified from the 5-km event and Monday's 10-km, the second part of the pursuit event, in which she came sixth.

Her gold medal from Sunday was awarded to Russian Yelena Vialbe, who came second in the race. Italian Stefania Belmondo and Russian Olga Danilova, who were third and fourth respectively, will get silver and bronze.
Yegorova will also be barred from taking part in the remaining world championships' races, Kasper said.
Bromantan was at the centre of a controversy at last year's summer Olympic games in Atlanta where several doping cases involving the drug were rejected on juridical grounds.
An arbitration panel overturned the sanctions after ruling athletes might had taken it to boost their immune system, not their performance.
After continuing allegations of blood doping in Nordic-skiing, FIS has introduced pre-race blood tests to detect abnormally high haemoglobin levels at this year's world championships.
But medical sources said Yegorova's case had nothing to do with blood doping as she was tested positive after undergoing a routine post-race urine test.

Yegorova had been struggling to recapture her best form since winning three golds at the 1994 Olympics. After Lillehammer, she retired temporarily from competition to give birth to a little boy, Viktor. She later experienced health problems.
Her best result this winter until the world championships was third place in a World Cup race last month in Kavgolovo, Russia.
"It was particularly difficult for me (to come back) because I'm not that young," she said after Sunday's race. "At one stage, I wondered if I would make it at all."
Ironically, after her victory, she had signed a statement handed to all winners by a Norwegian foundation fighting drugs and doping.
Asked her if she would allow the foundation to sell a signed poster of her, Yegorova wrote: "Yes, I support the work against dope and drugs..." And she signed.
